ImageDescription.value: Statue of Liberty (more formally, Liberty Enlightening the World, and more colloquially, Lady Liberty) is a structure located on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, presented to the United States on the centennial of the signing of the American Declaration of Independence as a gift from France. It was designed by Frédéric Bartholdi and gets its green coloring from patination of the outer copper covering. The statue is world-renowned for being the first thing sea-borne visitors, immigrants, and returning Americans see upon entering New York Harbor and has been known as a beacon of freedom to much of the world. It earned UNESCO World Heritage Site status in 1984.

Categories.value: Self-published work|Large images|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 missing SDC copyright license|Creative Commons Attribution missing SDC copyright status|Self-published work missing SDC copyright license|Images with Python source code|PNG created with Matplotlib|Asteroid belt

ImageDescription.value:
Plot of the position in space, as of the instant of midnight Teph 16 May 2026, of 1,522,030 asteroids, mostly in the asteroid belt. Positions of asteroids, the inner planets, and Jupiter are in the J2000 ecliptic frame, with the z-axis normal to Earth's orbit as of 1 January 2000 and the x-axis oriented toward the March equinox. For planets, positions should be exact (from JPL DE440). For minor bodies, positions are extrapolated from other epochs (mostly MJD 61200.0, 9 June 2026) assuming purely Keplerian motion.

The size of each marked asteroid is scaled to the square root of its diameter; these sizes are not to scale with the orbital distances shown in the chart. The asteroid belt is almost entirely empty space.

Colors show the asteroids' main dynamical categories.

  • Yellow: Near-Earth asteroids, including Amors, Apollos, Atens, and Atiras, as well as Mars-crossers with a < 1.7 au.
  • Orange: Other asteroids inside the main belt, chiefly Hungarias.
  • White: Main-belt asteroids, with the three main regions of the belt distinguished by slight shading.
  • Light blue: Outer main-belt, including Cybele asteroids.
  • Purple: Hilda asteroids and the Thule family (in 3:2 and 4:3 resonance with Jupiter).
  • Pink: Trojan asteroids, occupying Jupiter's L4 and L5 Lagrange points.
  • Green: Comets and comet-like objects, including Centaurs, damocloids, and a few asteroids in unusual orbits.

For about 130,000 asteroids, the diameter drawn is derived from actual measurements, obtained via stellar occultation, thermal emission, or direct imaging. For all others, the size of the plotted circle represents the assumed diameter based on the mean albedo for each dynamical category.

Size and orbital data is from JPL Solar System Dynamics (16 August 2026): https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/tools/sbdb_query.html
